title: Lucky Number 7
text:
Many people across centuries and cultures believed 7 to be a lucky number. There is also a movie made on this theme. There are many theories explaining why 7 became so popular - from religious to mathematical. Every religion has something to do with 7. But even before these religions came into existence, there was a simple game called dice, which I will conjecture as an explanation to why 7 came to be considered as lucky. Here, is a statistical theory.
The symmetrical dice that we play with today has its origins 3000 years ago in the Indus Valley Civilisation.



Maybe for thrill, people often played with two dice. Even Shakuni in Mahabharata.



Here are the 36 possible combinations we can see when we throw two dice:

# All possible outcomes of two dice

Sum of two dice thus becomes an important variable for all the players and gamblers. That sum will determine how far your pawns move in Ludo. In statistical lingo, it is the Random Variable (X) and it can take values between 2 (1+1) to 12 (6+6)

Clearly, a few sums are more frequently obtained than others. 2 is obtained only when both dice show 1 and it can happen only once. But 4 can be obtained with 2+2 and also 1+3 and 3+1. We can count them and also calculate the probability of obtaining a particular sum.

from collections import Counter

# Count frequencies
counts = Counter(sums)
counts

Counter({7: 6, 6: 5, 8: 5, 5: 4, 9: 4, 4: 3, 10: 3, 3: 2, 11: 2, 2: 1, 12: 1})




Show hidden code that calculates the PMF
# Total outcomes
total = len(outcomes)

# Probability distribution function
pmf = {k: v / total for k, v in sorted(counts.items())}

# Print result
for k, v in pmf.items():
    print(f"P(X = {k}) = {v:.3f}")

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = list(pmf.keys())
y = list(pmf.values())

# Plot

plt.xlabel("Sum of Two Dice")
plt.ylabel("Probability")

To see sum 7 thus has the most probability. 6 of the 36 possibilities help in getting that sum: 1+6, 6+1, 2+5, 5+2, 3+4, 4+3. The players and gamblers who believed in 7 more would have obviously won more, on an average. And my conjecture is that this allowed 7 to remain popular as a lucky number.

title: When to give up?
text:
The advice about giving up is mixed and confusing. One school of thinkers, singers and hustlers advice us to ‘Never Give Up’. And then there is this TEDx video about Art of Quitting I really like. Statistics has some advice as well. Let’s see if it can give us some clarity.
We’ll take our dice again. We know that each number has an equal probability of 1/6. We will consider getting a 6 as a success. The question is when do we give up trying to get a 6? Or, put differently, how many throws will it take to get the first 6? First success!

The probability of getting the first 6 in first throw is \(P(X=1) = 1/6\).
The probability of getting the first 6 in second throw is \(P(X=2) = 5/6 * 1/6\) (Not getting a 6 in first throw AND getting a 6 on second throw)
Thus the probability of getting the first 6 in nth throw is: \(P(X=n) = (5/6)^{n-1} * 1/6\) … a geometric progession.

We can plot these probabilities as follows. Lets assume that we threw the dice 30 times.

p = 1/6  # probability of success
pmf = {}

for i in range(1, 31):
    pmf[i] = (1 - p)**(i - 1) * p



Show hidden code that plots the PMF
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = list(pmf.keys())
y = list(pmf.values())

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10,7))
plt.bar(x, y)

plt.xlabel("Throw")
plt.ylabel("Probability of first 6 occuring")
plt.title("PMF of Throw on which first 6 occurs")
plt.xticks(x)

plt.show()









Ever heard about beginners luck? This chart shows you that. We actually have more chance of getting a 6, a success, on our first attempt.
Anyways, we were interested in a different question of: How many throws will it take to get the first 6?

The probability of getting a six in one throw: \(P(X=1)\)
The probability of getting a six in two throws \(P(X<=2) = P(X=1) + P(X=2)\)
The probability of getting a six in n throws \(P(X<=n) = P(X=1) + P(X=2) ..... + P(X=n)\)

We are calculating the cumulative probabilities. CDF.

import numpy as np
cumulative_probabilities = np.cumsum(np.array(list(pmf.values())))

cdf = {}
for i in range(1, 31):
    cdf[i] = cumulative_probabilities[i-1]



Show hidden code that plots the CDF
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
x = list(cdf.keys())
y = list(cdf.values())

# Plot
plt.figure(figsize=(10,7))
plt.step(x, y, where='post')

plt.xlabel("Throw")
plt.ylabel("Cumulative Probability")
plt.title("CDF of throws required to get the first 6")
plt.xticks(x)

plt.show()









There are some philosophical lessons here.

The probability of getting your first success increases with every try. Yes, you had the most chance on your first try. But that doesn’t mean you give up after the first try. It adds up. Go listen to that Never Give up Song
You can never be sure of 100% success. The Cumulative probability goes near 1, but reaches 1 only when n-> infinite. After throwing the dice for 30 times, there is 99.6% chance that you saw your first 6 in those 30 throws. Not 100%.


cdf[30]

np.float64(0.9957872797669126)


If we cannot give you 100% chance of getting a 6 on dice, you can forget about other life endeavours. We cannot take action in life asking 100% assurance. Neither from your doctor or lover. A better metric to ask for is expected value or mean.

#expected value or mean
expected_value = 0
for (k,v) in pmf.items():
    expected_value = expected_value + k*v

expected_value

5.848342071608855


I would interpret it that one should atleast try 6 throws before giving up on getting a 6. From CDF, we can see that there is about 66% chance to get the first 6 in 6 throws.

cdf[6]

np.float64(0.6651020233196159)


Or, a more conservative metric in this context is median. The cumulative probability of getting first 6 in 4 throws is about 52%. So, to have atleast 50% chance of success, one must throw dice 4 times at the least.

cdf[4]

np.float64(0.5177469135802469)


The Art of Quitting begins after these 4 or 6 attempts. But since many of us start thinking about giving up after the first attempt only, Never Give up advice holds for most of us.
